_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine -- Washington holiday calendars, 2026-2031. Loaded
through add_holidays alongside sql/sairnlaw_deadline_seed_washington.json.
== WASHINGTON IS THE ONE STATE THAT ANSWERS THE HOLIDAY QUESTION OUTRIGHT ==
Every other jurisdiction seeded so far has needed a judgment call about which
list of holidays a court rule means. Washington does not. CR 6(a) says it, in
six words, in the middle of the computation rule: "Legal holidays are
prescribed in RCW 1.16.050."
That is an EXPRESS cross-reference, not an inference. Contrast:
Texas       Tex. R. Civ. P. 4 says "legal holiday" and never cites
Gov't Code 662.021; the link is settled reading only.
Kentucky    RAP 6(A) and KRS 446.030 both say it and neither defines it,
and the candidate statute is not even titled "legal holidays".
N. Carolina Rule 6(a) asks a different question entirely -- whether the
COURTHOUSE IS CLOSED -- so its statute is the wrong source.
W. Virginia two rules define it two different ways inside one state.
Washington needed none of that reasoning. The rule names the statute.
== AND THE STATUTE EXCLUDES ITS OWN DECOYS, EXPRESSLY ======================
READ THIS BEFORE ADDING ANY DATE BELOW. RCW 1.16.050 contains TWO lists. Only
the first is legal holidays.
1.16.050(1)  "The following are state legal holidays" -- the eleven days
encoded here, plus Sunday (see below).
1.16.050(7)  "The legislature declares that the following days are
recognized as provided in this subsection, BUT MAY NOT BE
CONSIDERED LEGAL HOLIDAYS FOR ANY PURPOSE."
Subsection (7) is where Columbus Day, Pearl Harbor Day, Purple Heart
Recipient Recognition Day, Marcus Whitman Day, Public Lands Day, Washington
State Children's Day and a dozen more live. They are in the same statute CR
6(a) points at, and encoding them would roll deadlines LATER than the truth --
the direction that misses a filing. The statute forecloses that itself, in the
words "for any purpose", so this is not even a judgment call. It is only a
trap for anyone who regenerates the calendar from the section as a whole
rather than from subsection (1).
== SUNDAY IS A LEGAL HOLIDAY IN WASHINGTON, AND IS DELIBERATELY NOT LISTED ==
RCW 1.16.050(1)(a) is, in its entirety, "Sunday". Every Sunday of the year is
a state legal holiday. No Sunday appears below, for two reasons and neither is
an oversight: the engine already excludes Saturdays and Sundays through
isWeekend() before it ever consults a calendar, so listing 52 Sundays a year
would change no computed date; and CR 6(a) itself names "a Saturday, a Sunday
or a legal holiday" as three separate things, so the rule does not rely on
(1)(a) either. Note the drafting detail this explains: 1.16.050(5)(a) shifts a
holiday falling on a Sunday to the following Monday "OTHER THAN SUNDAY" --
the carve-out exists precisely because Sunday is itself on the list, and
without it every Sunday would shift itself onto every Monday.
RCW 1.16.050(5), verbatim: "Whenever any state legal holiday: (a) Other than
Sunday, falls upon a Sunday, the following Monday is the legal holiday; or
(b) Falls upon a Saturday, the preceding Friday is the legal holiday." Only
the fixed-date holidays can shift at all: 1 January, 19 June, 4 July,
11 November and 25 December.
THE BACKWARD SHIFT PUTS A HOLIDAY IN THE PREVIOUS YEAR. When 1 January falls
on a Saturday the legal holiday is Friday 31 December, which belongs to the
earlier year's calendar. 2027-12-31 is filed under 2027 here for that reason,
and deliberately NOT also under 2028 -- the engine resolves a holiday by the
year of the DATE and the endpoint rejects a date whose year does not match its
calendar, so a 2028-filed entry would be silently unreachable. That is why
2028 has ten entries below and the other years have eleven or twelve.
== NATIVE AMERICAN HERITAGE DAY IS A REAL LEGAL HOLIDAY HERE ===============
1.16.050(1)(k), "The Friday immediately following the fourth Thursday in
November, to be known as Native American Heritage Day." The day after
Thanksgiving is a statutory legal holiday in Washington. It is NOT one in
several states already seeded -- Illinois's M.R. 5272 adds it as a court
closure while the statute omits it, and Pennsylvania's calendars exclude it
outright -- so this is a real per-state difference, not a pattern.
JUNETEENTH IS A LEGAL HOLIDAY HERE, unlike in West Virginia's civil rules
where it is absent from both the rule and the code. 1.16.050(1)(f) names it.
1.16.050(2)'s one additional paid holiday per employee, and (3)'s two unpaid
holidays for reasons of faith or conscience: both are EMPLOYEE entitlements
chosen individually, not days the courts close, and neither is a legal holiday
under (1). Nothing is encoded for them.
Local court closures. CR 6(a) reaches time prescribed "by the local rules of
any superior court", and a county courthouse closed for weather or emergency
is not enumerable in advance. Same treatment as Michigan and North Carolina; a
deadline computed across such a closure is EARLY, never late.

authority.citation: RCW 1.16.050(1) (state legal holidays), applied to civil time computation by Wash. Super. Ct. Civ. R. 6(a)
authority.note: Generated 2026-08-25 from RCW 1.16.050(1), read verbatim from the Washington State Legislature's own site, and applied to civil time computation by CR 6(a), which says expressly "Legal holidays are prescribed in RCW 1.16.050" -- an express cross-reference, not an inference. ONLY SUBSECTION (1) IS ENCODED. Subsection (7) of the same section lists Columbus Day, Pearl Harbor Day, Purple Heart Recipient Recognition Day, Marcus Whitman Day, Public Lands Day, Washington State Children's Day and others as days that are "recognized ... but may not be considered legal holidays FOR ANY PURPOSE"; encoding them would roll deadlines LATE. Sunday is a legal holiday under (1)(a) and is deliberately absent -- the engine excludes weekends before consulting a calendar, so listing it would change no date, and 1.16.050(5)(a)'s "other than Sunday" carve-out exists for exactly that reason. Weekend shift is both-way per 1.16.050(5): Sunday -> following Monday, Saturday -> preceding Friday. Native American Heritage Day (the Friday after Thanksgiving) and Juneteenth are BOTH real statutory legal holidays here, which is not true of every state already seeded. Local superior court closures are not enumerable and are not included; a deadline computed across one is EARLY, never late.
